lesson.title: Ask, Don't Wait: Non-Blocking I/O
lesson.summary: Putting a socket into non-blocking mode makes send and receive calls return immediately, even when there is nothing to do yet, trading the simplicity of blocking I/O for control over when a thread actually waits.
lesson.body:
A socket can be switched out of its default blocking behavior into non-blocking mode, on POSIX systems typically through fcntl() with the O_NONBLOCK flag. Once a socket is non-blocking, recv() no longer puts the calling thread to sleep when there is no data available. Instead it returns immediately with a special error, conventionally EWOULDBLOCK or EAGAIN, telling the caller that nothing is available right now and to try again later. A send() call on a non-blocking socket behaves the same way if the outgoing buffer is full: rather than pausing the thread, it returns immediately and reports that it could not accept the data yet.

This is a genuinely different model from blocking I/O, not just a faster version of it. With blocking I/O, the operating system decides when a thread runs again, waking it only once the operation can actually complete. With non-blocking I/O, the operating system never puts the thread to sleep on that operation at all, and the responsibility for figuring out when to try again shifts entirely onto the program. A program using non-blocking sockets naively might just call recv() over and over in a tight loop until it finally gets data, but that busy-waits the CPU, burning a full core checking a socket that has nothing new to offer, potentially thousands of times a second for no benefit.

The real value of non-blocking mode is not looping on one socket, it is that a single thread can hold many sockets open at once without any of them being able to stall it. Because no call ever blocks, a thread can walk through a list of connections, try a recv() on each one, take whatever data is ready, skip the ones that are not, and move on, all without ever getting stuck waiting on a slow or idle peer. This is the piece that finally breaks the one-thread-per-connection limit that blocking I/O runs into: instead of needing a thread per client, a program needs one thread that keeps cycling through all of them.

The practical problem is efficiency. Naively checking every socket in a loop still wastes CPU on sockets that are not ready, and it does not tell a program when it should actually check, so if the loop does not run constantly it introduces delay. What is really needed is a way for the operating system to tell the program which sockets, out of many, are actually ready right now, so the program only spends time on the ones worth touching. That capability, readiness notification across a whole set of sockets, is exactly what select() and poll() provide, covered next.
